item.content:encoded:
I think in large part, this is one of those where the anomaly is more that it exists and provides information about other anomalies. Level 5 and Room 501 are definite anomalies, though:

There's the anachronistic material for the chains and door- my guess for the redaction is high carbon steel, or possibly a steel alloy like stainless steel or a tungsten alloy. High-carbon steel didn't even enter the scene until Southern India came up with Wootz Steel around 500 BC, and started exporting it to both the East and West, so finding anything like that in a 4500 year old structure is interesting to say the least.

There's also the 80000 kg granite slab engraved in an unknown language: Not impossible, but the sort of thing that would get attention. They still aren't quite certain how the Egyptians managed to work granite without steel at about the same time period, and that is a hell of a big block to transport to an area without significant granite deposits.

Add that to the fact that whatever was chained up in there only escaped about 20 years ago and might be SCP-682, and that the stuff they have translated about that block implies that it's plugging a hellgate of some sort, and it's definitely a good idea to keep an eye on it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The other one had a lot of potential, and I upvoted for that.

This one delivers on its potential, and it keeps the upvote.

Specific things I like:

1) You aren't trying to be subtle and hint at just what the SCP is about, but come right out and state that it's an ancient containment site. That allows a lot of details to be heaped on without 'giving away' the premise, and I think the article is stronger for it.

2) There's enough hinting about the prisoner to suggest a few possible backgrounds, but not enough to really determine exactly what it can do. Likewise, the door/portal concept, and it's not even clear if you need both the prisoner and the blocked doorway for the latter to be dangerous. The uncertainty is a good addition.

3) The suggestion that somehow the containment held until recently. It's not implied, but I prefer to read it as the broken containment is what caused the Foundation to discover SCP-557. While including more about the containment procedures would be best left to the imagination, I think some kind of 'how did we find this?' note would be a good addition.

I like most of it, with a couple of things I personally am not fond of but leave up to the consensus of my peers whether they're good or bad:

  • Making SCP-557-A reptilian, with that description, makes it sound a little too familiar…
  • I'm not in love with the prisoner already having escaped, but that's very much a matter of taste and/or judgement call, and others may strongly prefer it.

item.content:encoded:
I look forward to seing your creations :)

Seriously, the main reason I did this rewrite in the first place was that I loved the concept from Gabriel Jade's original, and felt that it fills an otherwise vacant conceptual niche. After all, with however many hundred SCPs currently posted, I can't think of any that describe containment (or attempted containment) by anyone prior to the Foundation's involvement, and I find it hard to believe that the Foundation wouldn't have had at least some spiritual ancestors.

One tip: At least in my opinion, this works best if the containment structure is 2000+ years old. For one thing, it's more compelling to think of some poor Bronze Age or earlier group trying to contain something without the benefits of modern technology. Second, consider how well many stone structures from back then have survived - ancient stoneworkers built stuff to last, even if there's a little cosmetic damage here and there.
